content.text:
Base directory for this skill: <home>/github/crit-7hw.6/plugin/skills/crit-loop

# The fix loop

The design-critic skill judges a picture of a design and writes a work order: the findings, ranked, each with where it is, what the viewer meets, the target, and the check that closes it. This skill tells you how to fix from that work order, how to check each fix, and when to stop. The critics decide every finding, rank, and status. You do not judge them again. The rules are FR-82 in `docs/PRD.md` of the deskcrit repository.

In the steps below, `<design-critic folder>` is the `design-critic` folder next to this skill's folder, and `<loop folder>` is a new folder in the system temp folder that holds one folder per round.

## Capture

Use the same capture in every round, so each round compares like with like.

- When you have the page source or a URL, capture with the measure script: `node <design-critic folder>/scripts/measure.mjs <page> --out <round folder>`. With no viewport flag it writes `desktop.png`, `phone.png`, `tablet.png`, `widescreen.png`, and `facts.json` into the round folder. Pick the flags in round 1: none, or the viewport flags the person asked for (`--desktop`, `--phone`, `--tablet`, `--widescreen`, `--width N`), and `--dark` when the person asks for dark mode or the code you changed touches the theme. Then pass exactly the same flags in every round, so each round captures the same viewports. Every screenshot that `facts.json` lists goes to the critic and to the work order, in the order of the facts file viewports. If round 1 found a dark mode and a later round's `facts.json` sets `dark_mode.found_by` to none, say at the stop that the fix broke dark mode. If it prints `cannot measure:` and exits with code 3 (the page does not open), use your own tool, as below, for the whole loop. If it exits with code 4, Playwright or its Chromium is missing: stop, show the person the install commands from the `cannot measure:` line, and ask whether to install them. Never install without their yes. On yes, run the install commands in the project, then run the measure script again. On no, use your own tool, as below, for the whole loop, and say at the stop that the loop ran without measured facts.
- Otherwise, take the screenshot with the tool you already have, such as Playwright or a browser tool, at the same viewport width and height and the same part of the page in every round, and save it in the round folder.

Rebuild or reload the app before each capture, so the image shows your fix and not the old build.

## Round 1: the crit

1. Capture into `<loop folder>/round-1`.
2. Run the design-critic skill on that capture, steps 1 to 5 of its `SKILL.md`, with every screenshot and the facts file when you have one. It writes `crit.md` and `work-order.json` into the round folder.
3. If the work order has no finding with a rank, stop: there is nothing to fix.

## Each round after that

1. Fix from the top of the last work order. Wait until the work-order agent has finished and the work order exists, and fix from it, not from `crit.md`: the work order has the measured places and targets that the prose leaves out. Take the findings in `rank` order. Each has a `location` (with a `selector` and a `box` when one was measured), a `target`, and a `fix_direction`. Fix as many as you can do well in one pass, from the top; the findings with `rank` null come last. Never add content; the last section of this file says what you may change in the copy.
   The rule against new content still holds, so a fix adds only an element that carries no content, such as a divider, a button that wraps an action already on the page, or a background. Before you commit such a fix, check the new element against the template tells. Open `<design-critic folder>/references/checklist.md`, find the "Template tells" section, and open the entries of each question there that the new element could fail with `node <design-critic folder>/scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`. When the element has a stock form that an entry names, such as a gradient, a glow, or a colored border, use a plain form instead: a solid color, a flat edge, a thin rule.
2. Capture into `<loop folder>/round-<n>`, the same way as in round 1.
3. Start a fresh recheck critic with the Agent tool: `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `model: "opus"`. Use this prompt, with the placeholders filled, and the facts line only when this round has a `facts.json`:

   ```
   Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

   Read <design-critic folder>/agents/recheck.md and follow it. The skill folder is <design-critic folder>; every path in recheck.md is relative to it.

   Before image: <absolute path of the last round's image>
   After image: <absolute path of this round's image>
   Last work order: <absolute path of the last work-order.json>
   Measured facts file: <absolute path of this round's facts.json>

   You critique only. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
   When the recheck is done, end with the full recheck as your final message. If you were spawned as a teammate, also call SendMessage to the agent that spawned you with the full recheck.
   ```

   With a facts file of several viewports, write `Before images: <absolute paths of the last round's screenshots>` and `After images: <absolute paths of this round's screenshots>` in place of the two image lines, both in the order of the facts file viewports.

4. Save its final message as `crit.md` in the round folder, exactly as it wrote it.
5. Count the findings it marked closed under "Finding status", and check the stop rule below. A finding marked "closed, new problem" counts as closed: your fix added a template tell, and the recheck lists that tell as a new problem, so the next work order holds it.
6. If you do not stop, write the new work order with step 5 of the design-critic skill's `SKILL.md`: this round's `crit.md`, this round's images, and its facts file. Then start the next round.

A finding marked worse is not progress. Fix it before the findings ranked below it.

## When to stop

Stop when one of these is true:

- The recheck has no ranked finding left: under "What would move it most" it says "None.".
- Two rounds in a row have no finding marked closed.

When you stop, tell the person:

- which of the two rules made you stop,
- the last first read and verdict,
- the findings still open or worse, with their places,
- the findings you left open because they need content that only the owner has, and what kind of content each one needs,
- the path of the loop folder.

If a script or a critic cannot run, do not retry it in a loop. Tell the person what it printed, and stop.

## Fix the design, not the score

Fix the design for the person who will use it. Do not hide or remove content to close a finding.

Never add content. Add no new text, facts, names, numbers, sample data, images, testimonials, or sections. Change the copy only with the editorial edits that a finding calls for: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear. Do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. Fix layout, type, color, spacing, and hierarchy freely. When a finding needs content that only the owner has, leave it open and tell the person at the stop.

commands.name: deskcrit:crit-loop
commands.description: (deskcrit) Use after you change UI code (HTML, CSS, components) and want to check the design and fix it. Runs the design-critic skill, fixes from the top of its work order, captures the page again at the same viewport, and has a fresh critic mark each finding closed, closed with a new problem, open, or worse, until no ranked finding is left or two rounds in a row close nothing.

commands.name: deskcrit:design-critic
commands.description: (deskcrit) Critiques still images of a design (a screenshot, mockup, poster, slide, chart, or illustration) the way a senior design director would in a crit, backed by a checklist of about 210 guidelines from Bringhurst, Müller-Brockmann, Tufte, WCAG, Nielsen and the rest of an approved reading list, plus 38 signs of an AI-made template from unslop. One image gets a crit. Two to twelve images get a crit each plus one check, which the request names: a consistency check of the set ("are these consistent") or a best pick ("which is best"). An agent caller must name one, or it gets a one-line refusal. Use when the user or the main thread wants a design critiqued, reviewed, or judged, asks "how does this look", "crit this", "what's wrong with this design", wants feedback on a screenshot before shipping, wants screens checked for consistency, or wants the best of several versions picked. Critiques only; it does not edit files or redesign the piece.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail
commands.description: (ponytail) Forces the laziest solution that actually works, simplest, shortest, most minimal. Channels a senior dev who has seen everything: question whether the task needs to exist at all (YAGNI), reach for the standard library before custom code, native platform features before dependencies, one line before fifty. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra. Use on ANY coding task: writing, adding, refactoring, fixing, reviewing, or designing code, and choosing libraries or dependencies. Also use whenever the user says "ponytail", "be lazy", "lazy mode", "simplest solution", "minimal solution", "yagni", "do less", or "shortest path", or complains about over-engineering, bloat, boilerplate, or unnecessary dependencies. Do NOT use for non-coding requests (general knowledge, prose, translation, summaries, recipes).

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-audit
commands.description: (ponytail) Whole-repo audit for over-engineering. Like ponytail-review, but scans the entire codebase instead of a diff: a ranked list of what to delete, simplify, or replace with stdlib/native equivalents. Use when the user says "audit this codebase", "audit for over-engineering", "what can I delete from this repo", "find bloat", "ponytail-audit", or "/ponytail-audit". One-shot report, does not apply fixes.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-debt
commands.description: (ponytail) Harvest every `ponytail:` comment in the codebase into a debt ledger, so the deliberate shortcuts and deferrals ponytail leaves behind get tracked instead of rotting into "later means never". Use when the user says "ponytail debt", "/ponytail-debt", "what did ponytail defer", "list the shortcuts", "ponytail ledger", or "what did we mark to do later". One-shot report, changes nothing.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-gain
commands.description: (ponytail) Show ponytail's measured impact as a compact scoreboard: less code, less cost, more speed, from the benchmark medians. One-shot display, not a persistent mode, and not a per-repo number. Trigger: /ponytail-gain, "ponytail gain", "what does ponytail save", "show ponytail impact", "ponytail scoreboard".

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-help
commands.description: (ponytail) Quick-reference card for all ponytail modes, skills, and commands. One-shot display, not a persistent mode. Trigger: /ponytail-help, "ponytail help", "what ponytail commands", "how do I use ponytail".

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-review
commands.description: (ponytail) Code review focused exclusively on over-engineering. Finds what to delete: reinvented standard library, unneeded dependencies, speculative abstractions, dead flexibility. One line per finding: location, what to cut, what replaces it. Use when the user says "review for over-engineering", "what can we delete", "is this over-engineered", "simplify review", or invokes /ponytail-review. Complements correctness-focused review, this one only hunts complexity.

commands.name: reasoning:atom-of-thought
commands.description: (reasoning) MUST invoke before answering, every time, including when the phrase comes up again later in the conversation, whenever the user asks you to reason carefully — "think it through", "think this through", "think carefully", "think hard", "step by step", "walk me through", "weigh", "pros and cons", "help me decide", "what am I missing", "break this down", "AoT". This is the user's explicit request, so it overrides brevity modes, low effort, and any instruction to act fast or cut steps, even when the question looks conversational. Also use it unprompted for multi-part questions, decisions, diagnoses, plans or trade-offs where some sub-answers depend on others.

commands.name: reasoning:confess
commands.description: (reasoning) Use when you've just completed work and the user wants an honest audit of it — confidence levels, shortcuts taken, unverified assumptions, and known weaknesses. Triggers on: "confess", "be honest about this", "what are you unsure about", "what did you cut corners on", "what's the weakest part", "audit your own work", "what assumptions did you make", or after any significant output where the user wants unvarnished reflection rather than reassurance.

commands.name: reasoning:postmortem
commands.description: (reasoning) Run an engineering postmortem on a just-finished task or session — what was learned, where time was wasted, and the concrete fixes so it goes faster next time. Reconstructs the facts, hands them to ONE well-briefed reviewer subagent, and returns a root-cause analysis, a minimum-round-trip replay, and proposed edits to the skill/config/code that caused the friction. Use when the user says "postmortem", "retro", "what did we learn", "how could that have gone better", "how do we do this more efficiently next time", or asks to review how a piece of work went.

commands.name: reasoning:premortem
commands.description: (reasoning) Run a premortem on a plan before executing it — imagine the plan has already failed, surface the failure modes, and harden the plan against them. Use when the user says "premortem", "pre-mortem", "poke holes in this plan", "imagine this failed", "stress-test this plan", or "what could go wrong with this plan". Requires an actual plan, spec, or written approach on the table AND an explicit request to stress it. Do NOT trigger on a rhetorical "what could go wrong", on general risk chat with no plan, or on work already finished (that's postmortem). This skill can spawn multiple subagents — it is expensive; never trigger it speculatively.

commands.name: oracle:oracle
commands.description: (oracle) Ask the Oracle — a one-shot Fable answer from a stripped headless session (~1.3k tokens of overhead vs ~6k for the oracle subagent), or, only when the user asks for Gemini, a one-shot Gemini 4 Carbon answer. Use when the user says "ask the oracle", "oracle,", or "/oracle <question>". Also use when the user says "ask Gemini", "gemini oracle", or "/oracle --gemini <question>".

commands.name: draft:critique
commands.description: (draft) Use this skill whenever someone wants feedback on a piece of writing without committing to changing it: essays, emails, board policies, internal docs, marketing copy, blog posts, or any prose draft. Trigger on phrases like "critique this", "how does this read?", "what's wrong with this", "give me notes on this", "review this draft", "does this land", "get me a second opinion on this", or "/critique [file]". This is a read-only pass — it never edits the file. If the user wants the writing actually fixed, not just assessed, use `tighten` instead.

commands.name: draft:skeleton
commands.description: (draft) Build a piece of writing from the inside out: core idea first, then one And, But, Therefore beat per section built from the But outward, then every topic sentence, then the joints between them, then headings, and only then the supporting prose. For essays, blog posts, memos, talks, long emails, anything where the argument has to hold. Works from nothing, from a pile of notes, or from an existing draft whose argument has come loose. Invoke explicitly as `/skeleton [file-or-notes] [auto]`, or when the user asks in their own words to "build the skeleton", "outline this properly", "work out the argument first", "write the topic sentences first", "reverse outline this", or "restructure this piece". Do NOT load this on a plain "write me a blog post" or "draft an email"; the six stages are a choice the writer makes, not a default. For prose whose argument is sound and whose words are fat, use `tighten`. For notes on a draft without changing it, use `critique`.

commands.name: draft:tighten
commands.description: (draft) Use this skill whenever someone hands you a piece of writing and wants it actually fixed: tightened, cut for economy, given a rigorous line edit. Essays, emails, board policies, internal docs, marketing copy, blog posts, or any prose draft. Applies every edit automatically, no approval step (at most a one-line calibration question on a long doc whose purpose is ambiguous) — the right call whenever the ask is "just make this better" and the user doesn't want to review each change. Trigger on phrases like "tighten this", "clean this up", "fix this", "edit this for economy", "make this leaner", "cut the fluff from this doc", "give this a line edit and apply it", "this feels bloated, fix it", or "/tighten [file]". Works on a single document or a batch in one run: several board policies, a folder of drafts, a stack of emails. If the user wants feedback without the file being changed, use `critique` instead. Don't reach for this when the request is to write something new, brainstorm, or restructure unprompted; it edits prose that already exists, it doesn't ghostwrite.

commands.name: typesafe:typesafe-ai
commands.description: (typesafe) Build AI-powered software with TypeSafe: small units of AI intelligence you can use like programming primitives. Its System One models, including Jev, turn natural language and application state into typed judgments and probabilities that code can combine. Use when a feature needs programmable common sense, when brainstorming what AI could make possible in an app, or when an LLM prompt-and-parse step could become a structured decision. Applications include routing, ranking, extraction, verification, and interactive experiences; these are starting points, not the limits. Read live docs and cookbooks to find useful patterns and discover new combinations.

commands.name: message:judge
commands.description: (message) Score a persuasive political message against the rulebook in references/rules.md, using Jev (TypeSafe's System One judgment model) to answer each rule's question, and turn the failures into concrete rewrite suggestions. Assumes a progressive messenger. Works on pasted text, a local file, a URL, a whole site (crawled), or an ordered series of messages read from one file. Trigger on "judge this message", "score this message", "make this more persuasive", "is this persuasive", "check this messaging", "review this campaign email", or "audit this candidate website".

commands.name: raindrop:raindrop
commands.description: (raindrop) Read and manage the user's Raindrop.io bookmarks through the Raindrop REST API. Use whenever the user mentions Raindrop, bookmarks, saved links, "what did I save about X", tags on saved links, highlights, or reading lists, or asks to save, tag, move, search, export, import, back up or clean up bookmarks. Covers every documented endpoint: bookmarks (called raindrops), collections, sharing, tags, highlights, filters, user, import, export, backups, file uploads and OAuth tokens.

commands.name: design
commands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Sync a React design system to Claude Design. Bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design."

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus broken CLAUDE.md rules and cleanups where the model's recipe covers them; see /simplify) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: claude-approvals
commands.description: Use BEFORE creating, changing, cleaning up or explaining a Claude Approvals policy file (.claude/approvals.yml) or custom classifier (.claude/classifiers/), or answering a question about its check, cost or speed. Edits that look harmless can let changes merge unreviewed. Also before or after anybody uninstalls or suspends the Claude GitHub App. Not for CODEOWNERS, branch protection, GitHub Actions or Claude Code's own permission settings.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: schedule
commands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read FIRST, before you answer, run a command or open a file (already started? read it now); don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file; if nothing hits, load this skill).

commands.name: deskcrit:design-critic
commands.description: (deskcrit) Critiques still images of a design (a screenshot, mockup, poster, slide, chart, or illustration) the way a senior design director would in a crit, backed by a checklist of about 210 guidelines from Bringhurst, Müller-Brockmann, Tufte, WCAG, Nielsen and the rest of an approved reading list, plus 38 signs of an AI-made template from unslop. One image gets a crit. Two to twelve images get a crit each plus one check, which the request names: a consistency check of the set ("are these consistent") or a best pick ("which is best"). An agent caller must name one, or it gets a one-line refusal. Use when the user or the main thread wants a design critiqued, reviewed, or judged, asks "how does this look", "crit this", "what's wrong with this design", wants feedback on a screenshot before shipping, wants screens checked for consistency, or wants the best of several versions picked. Critiques only; it does not edit files or redesign the piece.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail
commands.description: (ponytail) Forces the laziest solution that actually works, simplest, shortest, most minimal. Channels a senior dev who has seen everything: question whether the task needs to exist at all (YAGNI), reach for the standard library before custom code, native platform features before dependencies, one line before fifty. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra. Use on ANY coding task: writing, adding, refactoring, fixing, reviewing, or designing code, and choosing libraries or dependencies. Also use whenever the user says "ponytail", "be lazy", "lazy mode", "simplest solution", "minimal solution", "yagni", "do less", or "shortest path", or complains about over-engineering, bloat, boilerplate, or unnecessary dependencies. Do NOT use for non-coding requests (general knowledge, prose, translation, summaries, recipes).

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-audit
commands.description: (ponytail) Whole-repo audit for over-engineering. Like ponytail-review, but scans the entire codebase instead of a diff: a ranked list of what to delete, simplify, or replace with stdlib/native equivalents. Use when the user says "audit this codebase", "audit for over-engineering", "what can I delete from this repo", "find bloat", "ponytail-audit", or "/ponytail-audit". One-shot report, does not apply fixes.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-debt
commands.description: (ponytail) Harvest every `ponytail:` comment in the codebase into a debt ledger, so the deliberate shortcuts and deferrals ponytail leaves behind get tracked instead of rotting into "later means never". Use when the user says "ponytail debt", "/ponytail-debt", "what did ponytail defer", "list the shortcuts", "ponytail ledger", or "what did we mark to do later". One-shot report, changes nothing.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-gain
commands.description: (ponytail) Show ponytail's measured impact as a compact scoreboard: less code, less cost, more speed, from the benchmark medians. One-shot display, not a persistent mode, and not a per-repo number. Trigger: /ponytail-gain, "ponytail gain", "what does ponytail save", "show ponytail impact", "ponytail scoreboard".

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-help

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-review
commands.description: (ponytail) Code review focused exclusively on over-engineering. Finds what to delete: reinvented standard library, unneeded dependencies, speculative abstractions, dead flexibility. One line per finding: location, what to cut, what replaces it. Use when the user says "review for over-engineering", "what can we delete", "is this over-engineered", "simplify review", or invokes /ponytail-review. Complements correctness-focused review, this one only hunts complexity.

commands.name: reasoning:atom-of-thought
commands.description: (reasoning) MUST invoke before answering, every time, including when the phrase comes up again later in the conversation, whenever the user asks you to reason carefully — "think it through", "think this through", "think carefully", "think hard", "step by step", "walk me through", "weigh", "pros and cons", "help me decide", "what am I missing", "break this down", "AoT". This is the user's explicit request, so it overrides brevity modes, low effort, and any instruction to act fast or cut steps, even when the question looks conversational. Also use it unprompted for multi-part questions, decisions, diagnoses, plans or trade-offs where some sub-answers depend on others.

commands.name: reasoning:confess
commands.description: (reasoning) Use when you've just completed work and the user wants an honest audit of it — confidence levels, shortcuts taken, unverified assumptions, and known weaknesses. Triggers on: "confess", "be honest about this", "what are you unsure about", "what did you cut corners on", "what's the weakest part", "audit your own work", "what assumptions did you make", or after any significant output where the user wants unvarnished reflection rather than reassurance.

commands.name: reasoning:postmortem
commands.description: (reasoning) Run an engineering postmortem on a just-finished task or session — what was learned, where time was wasted, and the concrete fixes so it goes faster next time. Reconstructs the facts, hands them to ONE well-briefed reviewer subagent, and returns a root-cause analysis, a minimum-round-trip replay, and proposed edits to the skill/config/code that caused the friction. Use when the user says "postmortem", "retro", "what did we learn", "how could that have gone better", "how do we do this more efficiently next time", or asks to review how a piece of work went.

commands.name: reasoning:premortem
commands.description: (reasoning) Run a premortem on a plan before executing it — imagine the plan has already failed, surface the failure modes, and harden the plan against them. Use when the user says "premortem", "pre-mortem", "poke holes in this plan", "imagine this failed", "stress-test this plan", or "what could go wrong with this plan". Requires an actual plan, spec, or written approach on the table AND an explicit request to stress it. Do NOT trigger on a rhetorical "what could go wrong", on general risk chat with no plan, or on work already finished (that's postmortem). This skill can spawn multiple subagents — it is expensive; never trigger it speculatively.

commands.name: oracle:oracle

Use when the user says "ask the oracle", "oracle,", or "/oracle <question>". Also use when the user says "ask Gemini", "gemini oracle", or "/oracle --gemini <question>".

commands.name: draft:critique
commands.description: (draft) Use this skill whenever someone wants feedback on a piece of writing without committing to changing it: essays, emails, board policies, internal docs, marketing copy, blog posts, or any prose draft. Trigger on phrases like "critique this", "how does this read?", "what's wrong with this", "give me notes on this", "review this draft", "does this land", "get me a second opinion on this", or "/critique [file]". This is a read-only pass — it never edits the file. If the user wants the writing actually fixed, not just assessed, use `tighten` instead.

commands.name: draft:skeleton
commands.description: (draft) Build a piece of writing from the inside out: core idea first, then one And, But, Therefore beat per section built from the But outward, then every topic sentence, then the joints between them, then headings, and only then the supporting prose. For essays, blog posts, memos, talks, long emails, anything where the argument has to hold. Works from nothing, from a pile of notes, or from an existing draft whose argument has come loose. Invoke explicitly as `/skeleton [file-or-notes] [auto]`, or when the user asks in their own words to "build the skeleton", "outline this properly", "work out the argument first", "write the topic sentences first", "reverse outline this", or "restructure this piece". Do NOT load this on a plain "write me a blog post" or "draft an email"; the six stages are a choice the writer makes, not a default. For prose whose argument is sound and whose words are fat, use `tighten`. For notes on a draft without changing it, use `critique`.

commands.name: draft:tighten
commands.description: (draft) Use this skill whenever someone hands you a piece of writing and wants it actually fixed: tightened, cut for economy, given a rigorous line edit. Essays, emails, board policies, internal docs, marketing copy, blog posts, or any prose draft. Applies every edit automatically, no approval step (at most a one-line calibration question on a long doc whose purpose is ambiguous) — the right call whenever the ask is "just make this better" and the user doesn't want to review each change. Trigger on phrases like "tighten this", "clean this up", "fix this", "edit this for economy", "make this leaner", "cut the fluff from this doc", "give this a line edit and apply it", "this feels bloated, fix it", or "/tighten [file]". Works on a single document or a batch in one run: several board policies, a folder of drafts, a stack of emails. If the user wants feedback without the file being changed, use `critique` instead. Don't reach for this when the request is to write something new, brainstorm, or restructure unprompted; it edits prose that already exists, it doesn't ghostwrite.

commands.name: typesafe:typesafe-ai
commands.description: (typesafe) Build AI-powered software with TypeSafe: small units of AI intelligence you can use like programming primitives. Its System One models, including Jev, turn natural language and application state into typed judgments and probabilities that code can combine. Use when a feature needs programmable common sense, when brainstorming what AI could make possible in an app, or when an LLM prompt-and-parse step could become a structured decision. Applications include routing, ranking, extraction, verification, and interactive experiences; these are starting points, not the limits. Read live docs and cookbooks to find useful patterns and discover new combinations.

commands.name: message:judge

Assumes a progressive messenger. Works on pasted text, a local file, a URL, a whole site (crawled), or an ordered series of messages read from one file. Trigger on "judge this message", "score this message", "make this more persuasive", "is this persuasive", "check this messaging", "review this campaign email", or "audit this candidate website".

commands.name: raindrop:raindrop

commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". content.content:
1	---
2	name: design-critic
3	description: Critiques still images of a design (a screenshot, mockup, poster, slide, chart, or illustration) the way a senior design director would in a crit, backed by a checklist of about 210 guidelines from Bringhurst, Müller-Brockmann, Tufte, WCAG, Nielsen and the rest of an approved reading list, plus 38 signs of an AI-made template from unslop. One image gets a crit. Two to twelve images get a crit each plus one check, which the request names: a consistency check of the set ("are these consistent") or a best pick ("which is best"). An agent caller must name one, or it gets a one-line refusal. Use when the user or the main thread wants a design critiqued, reviewed, or judged, asks "how does this look", "crit this", "what's wrong with this design", wants feedback on a screenshot before shipping, wants screens checked for consistency, or wants the best of several versions picked. Critiques only; it does not edit files or redesign the piece.
4	---
5	
6	# Design critic
7	
8	This skill runs a critic agent on one image, or on the screenshots of one page at several viewports. The agent walks a checklist of guidelines, goes deep on anything that fails with the guideline's sources and approved fixes, then writes a ranked crit.
9	
10	## Pick the mode
11	
12	Count the images first. The count picks the mode, and nothing else does. The screenshots that one `facts.json` lists, one per viewport, count as one image: they are one page, so they get one normal crit and never start contact-sheet mode.
13	
14	- **One image: a normal crit.** Follow "Run it". The person gets one crit and one work order.
15	- **Two or more images: contact-sheet mode, always.** Follow "Contact-sheet mode". Each image gets its own normal crit and work order, and then one last agent reads all the images on one contact sheet. That last agent does one of two jobs, and the request picks which:
16	  - **Consistency check** (`agents/set-critic.md`): does the set hold together as one product, and which image breaks a pattern the others keep. Requests such as "are these consistent" or "check this flow" mean this.
17	  - **Best pick** (`agents/picker.md`): which version does the job best. Requests such as "which is best", "pick one", "compare v1 and v2", or "before and after" mean this. The old before-and-after compare is now the best pick with two images.
18	- **When the request does not say which**, ask the person one question that names the two: "Do you want a consistency check of the set, or a pick of the best version?" When the caller is another agent and no person can be asked, the caller must name the mode. If it did not, stop and reply with this one line, and do not guess: `Two or more images need a mode: "consistency check" or "best pick".`
19	- **Several images to critique with neither check**: call this skill once per image, each time with one image. Contact-sheet mode always adds the last agent.
20	- **At most twelve images.** The contact sheet holds twelve; with more, split the set or ask the person which twelve.
21	- **Cost.** Contact-sheet mode starts two Opus agents and one Sonnet agent per image, plus one Opus agent for the last step: five images start eleven Opus agents.
22	
23	## Run it
24	
25	1. Collect the inputs: the absolute path of each image, and whatever you know about the piece's purpose, audience, and medium. Do not ask the user for context they did not give; the critic states its own assumption.
26	2. Spawn one agent with the Agent tool: `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `model: "opus"`. Use this prompt, with the placeholders filled. `<skill folder>` is the base directory Claude Code gave when it loaded this skill.
27	
28	   ```
29	   Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
30	
31	   Read <skill folder>/agents/critic.md and follow it. The skill folder is <skill folder>; every path in critic.md is relative to it.
32	
33	   Image(s): <absolute paths>
34	   What I know about the piece: <purpose, audience, medium, or "nothing">
35	   <Any focus the caller asked for, such as "compare v1 and v2" or "only the chart". Omit if none.>
36	
37	   You critique only. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
38	   When the critique is done, end with the full critique as your final message. If you were spawned as a teammate, also call SendMessage to the agent that spawned you with the full critique.
39	   ```
40	
41	   If the person gives a page or a URL, run `scripts/measure.mjs` on it to get a facts file. Pass no viewport flag, so it renders its four default viewports, or the flags that pick the viewports the person asked for (`--desktop`, `--phone`, `--tablet`, `--widescreen`, `--width N`). Add `--dark` only when the person asks about dark mode, the theme, or both modes. With `--dark`, the script writes a `<name>-dark` entry and `<name>-dark.png` for each viewport only when the page has a dark mode, and `dark_mode.found_by` in `facts.json` says how it found it, or `none`. If it exits with code 4, Playwright or its Chromium is missing: show the person the install commands from its `cannot measure:` line, ask whether to install them, and never install without their yes. On no, critique the image alone and say so.
42	
43	   With a facts file, the critic gets every screenshot it lists in one crit. Put the absolute path of each viewport's `screenshot` on the `Image(s)` line, in the order of the facts file viewports, so each `<name>-dark.png` comes right after its light twin.
44	
45	   When you have a measured facts file for the page in the image (`facts.json` from `scripts/measure.mjs`), add this line right after the `Image(s)` line, with the path filled:
46	
47	   ```
48	   Measured facts file: <absolute path of facts.json>
49	   ```
50	
51	   When the `Image(s)` line names two or more viewports, add this line right after the `Measured facts file:` line, with the viewport names in the same order as the images:
52	
53	   ```
54	   Viewports, in image order: <names, such as desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen>
55	   ```
56	
57	3. Add the section "Where it could go further" with a second agent, which reads the image and the finished crit and writes only that section. Pick the work folder: the folder that holds `facts.json` when there is one, else the image's folder. Save the critique there as `crit.md`, exactly as the agent wrote it, with the Write tool. Then spawn one agent with the Agent tool: `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `model: "opus"`, with this prompt and the placeholders filled:
58	
59	   ```
60	   Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
61	
62	   Read <skill folder>/agents/go-further.md and follow it. The skill folder is <skill folder>; every path in go-further.md is relative to it.
63	
64	   Image(s): <absolute paths, as in step 2>
65	   Crit file: <absolute path of crit.md>
66	
67	   You write only the section. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
68	   End with the section as your final message. If you were spawned as a teammate, also call SendMessage to the agent that spawned you with the section.
69	   ```
70

---
name: design-critic
description: Critiques still images of a design (a screenshot, mockup, poster, slide, chart, or illustration) the way a senior design director would in a crit, backed by a checklist of about 210 guidelines from Bringhurst, Müller-Brockmann, Tufte, WCAG, Nielsen and the rest of an approved reading list, plus 38 signs of an AI-made template from unslop. One image gets a crit. Two to twelve images get a crit each plus one check, which the request names: a consistency check of the set ("are these consistent") or a best pick ("which is best"). An agent caller must name one, or it gets a one-line refusal. Use when the user or the main thread wants a design critiqued, reviewed, or judged, asks "how does this look", "crit this", "what's wrong with this design", wants feedback on a screenshot before shipping, wants screens checked for consistency, or wants the best of several versions picked. Critiques only; it does not edit files or redesign the piece.
---

# Design critic

This skill runs a critic agent on one image, or on the screenshots of one page at several viewports. The agent walks a checklist of guidelines, goes deep on anything that fails with the guideline's sources and approved fixes, then writes a ranked crit.

## Pick the mode

Count the images first. The count picks the mode, and nothing else does. The screenshots that one `facts.json` lists, one per viewport, count as one image: they are one page, so they get one normal crit and never start contact-sheet mode.

- **One image: a normal crit.** Follow "Run it". The person gets one crit and one work order.
- **Two or more images: contact-sheet mode, always.** Follow "Contact-sheet mode". Each image gets its own normal crit and work order, and then one last agent reads all the images on one contact sheet. That last agent does one of two jobs, and the request picks which:
  - **Consistency check** (`agents/set-critic.md`): does the set hold together as one product, and which image breaks a pattern the others keep. Requests such as "are these consistent" or "check this flow" mean this.
  - **Best pick** (`agents/picker.md`): which version does the job best. Requests such as "which is best", "pick one", "compare v1 and v2", or "before and after" mean this. The old before-and-after compare is now the best pick with two images.
- **When the request does not say which**, ask the person one question that names the two: "Do you want a consistency check of the set, or a pick of the best version?" When the caller is another agent and no person can be asked, the caller must name the mode. If it did not, stop and reply with this one line, and do not guess: `Two or more images need a mode: "consistency check" or "best pick".`
- **Several images to critique with neither check**: call this skill once per image, each time with one image. Contact-sheet mode always adds the last agent.
- **At most twelve images.** The contact sheet holds twelve; with more, split the set or ask the person which twelve.
- **Cost.** Contact-sheet mode starts two Opus agents and one Sonnet agent per image, plus one Opus agent for the last step: five images start eleven Opus agents.

## Run it

1. Collect the inputs: the absolute path of each image, and whatever you know about the piece's purpose, audience, and medium. Do not ask the user for context they did not give; the critic states its own assumption.
2. Spawn one agent with the Agent tool: `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `model: "opus"`. Use this prompt, with the placeholders filled. `<skill folder>` is the base directory Claude Code gave when it loaded this skill.

   ```
   Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

   Read <skill folder>/agents/critic.md and follow it. The skill folder is <skill folder>; every path in critic.md is relative to it.

   Image(s): <absolute paths>
   What I know about the piece: <purpose, audience, medium, or "nothing">
   <Any focus the caller asked for, such as "compare v1 and v2" or "only the chart". Omit if none.>

   You critique only. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
   When the critique is done, end with the full critique as your final message. If you were spawned as a teammate, also call SendMessage to the agent that spawned you with the full critique.
   ```

   If the person gives a page or a URL, run `scripts/measure.mjs` on it to get a facts file. Pass no viewport flag, so it renders its four default viewports, or the flags that pick the viewports the person asked for (`--desktop`, `--phone`, `--tablet`, `--widescreen`, `--width N`). Add `--dark` only when the person asks about dark mode, the theme, or both modes. With `--dark`, the script writes a `<name>-dark` entry and `<name>-dark.png` for each viewport only when the page has a dark mode, and `dark_mode.found_by` in `facts.json` says how it found it, or `none`. If it exits with code 4, Playwright or its Chromium is missing: show the person the install commands from its `cannot measure:` line, ask whether to install them, and never install without their yes. On no, critique the image alone and say so.

   With a facts file, the critic gets every screenshot it lists in one crit. Put the absolute path of each viewport's `screenshot` on the `Image(s)` line, in the order of the facts file viewports, so each `<name>-dark.png` comes right after its light twin.

   When you have a measured facts file for the page in the image (`facts.json` from `scripts/measure.mjs`), add this line right after the `Image(s)` line, with the path filled:

   ```
   Measured facts file: <absolute path of facts.json>
   ```

   When the `Image(s)` line names two or more viewports, add this line right after the `Measured facts file:` line, with the viewport names in the same order as the images:

   ```
   Viewports, in image order: <names, such as desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen>
   ```

3. Add the section "Where it could go further" with a second agent, which reads the image and the finished crit and writes only that section. Pick the work folder: the folder that holds `facts.json` when there is one, else the image's folder. Save the critique there as `crit.md`, exactly as the agent wrote it, with the Write tool. Then spawn one agent with the Agent tool: `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `model: "opus"`, with this prompt and the placeholders filled:

   ```
   Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

   Read <skill folder>/agents/go-further.md and follow it. The skill folder is <skill folder>; every path in go-further.md is relative to it.

   Image(s): <absolute paths, as in step 2>
   Crit file: <absolute path of crit.md>

   You write only the section. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
   End with the section as your final message. If you were spawned as a teammate, also call SendMessage to the agent that spawned you with the section.
   ```

   Join the section into the crit exactly as the agent wrote it, as its own paragraph right after "What's working": before "Couldn't judge from a still" when the crit has it, else before "Checklist". Write the joined crit over `crit.md`.

4. Give the critique to the user, joined with the section. Do not soften or trim it. Add your own comment only if the user asked for it.

5. Write the work order, the JSON a coding agent acts on (schema: `schemas/work-order.schema.json` in the deskcrit repository). Use the `crit.md` of step 3; the work-order agent leaves the items of "Where it could go further" out. Then spawn one agent with the Agent tool: `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `model: "sonnet"`, with this prompt, the placeholders filled, and the facts line only when the critic had that file:

   ```
   Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

   Read <skill folder>/agents/work-order.md and follow it. The skill folder is <skill folder>; every path in work-order.md is relative to it.

   Crit file: <absolute path of crit.md>
   Image(s): <absolute paths, as in step 2>
   Measured facts file: <absolute path of facts.json>
   Write in: <absolute path of the work folder>

   When the work order is done, end with its absolute path as your final message. If you were spawned as a teammate, also call SendMessage to the agent that spawned you with that path.
   ```

   Tell the user the path of `work-order.json`. A work order is for one page, with all its viewports, so in contact-sheet mode each page gets its own.

## Contact-sheet mode

Use this mode for two or more images, once you know the mode from "Pick the mode". The person gets one crit and one work order per image, and then one consistency check or one best pick.

1. For each image, run "Run it" steps 1, 2, 3, and 5 with that one image (for a page with a facts file, all of its viewports), so each crit has its "Where it could go further" section and its work order: spawn all the critics in one message so they run at the same time, use the usual prompt, and when each crit is done, write its work order in its own work folder (the folder that holds that image's `facts.json`, else a new folder per image in the system temp folder, so no two work orders share a folder).
2. At the same time, make the contact sheet. Run `node <skill folder>/scripts/contact-sheet.mjs <image paths in order> --out <new folder in the system temp folder>`, with one image per page: for a page with a facts file, its first screenshot, which is `desktop.png` unless the viewport flags left desktop out. Use the same images on the `Images, in tile order` line below. It writes `sheet.png` and `tiles.json` in that folder. Then spawn one agent with the Agent tool: `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `model: "opus"`, with this prompt and the placeholders filled. `<agent file>` is `set-critic.md` for the consistency check and `picker.md` for the best pick.

   ```
   Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

   Read <skill folder>/agents/<agent file> and follow it. The skill folder is <skill folder>; every path in <agent file> is relative to it.

   Contact sheet: <absolute path of sheet.png>
   Tiles file: <absolute path of tiles.json>
   Images, in tile order: <absolute paths>
   What I know about the piece: <purpose, audience, medium, or "nothing">

   You critique only. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
   When the crit is done, end with the full crit as your final message. If you were spawned as a teammate, also call SendMessage to the agent that spawned you with the full crit.
   ```

   When the person gave the pages themselves (a URL or an HTML file for each) and `scripts/measure.mjs` ran on each, also run `node <skill folder>/scripts/compare-facts.mjs <facts.json of each page, in tile order> --out <folder>/differences.json`. It writes the differences across pages in measured numbers (content left edge, text width, type sizes, text colors). Add this line to the prompt right after the `Images, in tile order` line, with the path filled. When there are no pages, or it exits with a usage error, leave the line out.

   ```
   Measured differences file: <absolute path of differences.json>
   ```

   The consistency check and the best pick get no work order.
3. Give the person the consistency check or the best pick first, then each image's crit under its file name, as the agents wrote them, then the path of each `work-order.json`.

## What is in the folder

- `agents/critic.md`: the critic's instructions, how it looks, what makes a good finding, and the output format.
- `references/checklist.md`: yes-or-no questions in sections, whole page first and detail last, where yes means fine; each kind of defect has one question, and each question points to the full entries it stands for.
- `references/<domain>.md`: full entries for basics, layout, typography, color, art direction, ux, accessibility, and dataviz. Each gives the rule, what to look for, the source, caveats about the source, and the approved fix.
- `agents/deep-mode.md`, `agents/section-critic.md`, `agents/director.md`, and `references/checklist-<section>.md`: the deep mode, one critic per checklist section and a director who merges and ranks their reports.
- `agents/go-further.md`: the instructions of the second agent, which reads the image and the finished crit and writes only the section "Where it could go further".
- `agents/work-order.md`: the instructions of the agent that turns the finished crit into `work-order.json`.
- `scripts/work-order.mjs`: checks a work order against its crit, image, and facts file: one entry per ranked finding, and every pixel box taken from the facts file or a crop.
- `agents/set-critic.md`: the consistency check of contact-sheet mode, which judges whether a set of images keeps one pattern and names each image that breaks it.
- `agents/picker.md`: the best pick of contact-sheet mode, which ranks the versions by how well each does the job and names the best one.
- `scripts/compare-facts.mjs`: compares the facts files of the pages of one set and writes the measured differences across pages (FR-84), checked by `schemas/facts-diff.schema.json`.
- `scripts/contact-sheet.mjs`: lays several PNG screens out as one numbered contact sheet and writes `tiles.json`, which maps each tile number to its file.
- `agents/recheck.md`: the recheck critic of the crit-loop skill, which checks a fix against the last work order.
- `scripts/build.rb`: makes `references/` from this repository's `GUIDELINES.md` and `packs/`.

## Update the references

The references come from the repository root (`GUIDELINES.md` and `packs/<pack>/pack.yaml`). Do not edit `references/` by hand. When the catalog or a pack changes, run this from the repository root:

```
ruby plugin/skills/design-critic/scripts/build.rb
```

The installed plugin copy has no `GUIDELINES.md`, so run it from a checkout of the repository. `npm run ci` checks that the committed references equal a fresh build.

The script fails if a crit criterion has no matching guideline entry.
